Read the passage carefully and choose the best answer A, B C or D.

Growing up in the late 1970s, my world was defined by the steady, rhythmic ticking of a hundred different
hearts. We lived in a small, stilted house on the outskirts of Taiping, Perak, where the rain fell almost
every afternoon. My father was a watchmaker, a man of incredible patience who operated a cramped
workshop attached to the front of our home. While other children played football in the muddy fields, I
spent my afternoons tucked away in a dusty corner, fascinated by the tiny, shining pieces of brass and
steel that lay scattered across his workbench like fallen stars.
The workshop was a place of quiet intensity. It smelled of fine machine oil and aged wood. Dad did
not have the advanced tools of modern watch experts; instead, he relied on a single magnifying glass held
tightly in his eye and a set of tweezers that seemed like extensions of his own fingers. I would sit for
hours, watching his steady hands. He would take apart a rusted watch, cleaning each tiny screw and gear
with such focus that he often forgot to drink the coffee my mother left for him. He used a small brush to
remove every speck of dust, explaining that even a single hair could stop a clock's heart. To me, his ability
to bring a broken object back to life was a complete miracle.
Times were often difficult. In those days, people only repaired watches when they absolutely had to,
and Dad's income was unstable. There were months when the "special" Sunday meal was simply extra
sardines in the tomato sauce, shared carefully among my parents, my two sisters, and me. Yet, Dad never
let the weight of our financial struggle ruin the atmosphere of the workshop. He would whistle old P.
Ramlee tunes as he worked, his face showing deep concentration but his eyes reflecting a sense of pride.
He believed that if you treated an object with respect, it would serve you forever—a belief he applied to
our family as well. He taught us that a broken situation, like a broken clock, just needed time and a gentle
hand to fix.
When I was eleven, a major electronics factory opened in Selangor, and Dad was offered a job as a
skilled technician. It was a chance for a steady salary, but it meant leaving our breezy wooden home for
a crowded low-cost flat in Petaling Jaya. The change was a shock to our system. The flat was incredibly
hot, and the noise of the city was a harsh contrast to the quiet nights in Taiping. Dad's workshop was
gone, replaced by a cold, air-conditioned factory floor where he wore a white coat and worked under
bright lights. He became quieter, his shoulders slumped as he travelled to work on an old motorbike
through the heavy traffic. He missed the freedom of his own workbench, but he never complained,
knowing this sacrifice was the only way to pay for our education and future.
Slowly, our situation improved. Dad's skill in detailed work led to a promotion, and eventually, he
opened his own specialist clock shop in a high-end shopping mall. By the time I entered university, we
had moved into a large double-storey house in a quiet suburb. The "workshop" was now a modern studio
in the back garden, equipped with better cleaning machines and high-quality tools. For Dad, the days of
working under a dim yellow bulb were over. The ease with which he could now get spare parts from

across the globe was a source of constant wonder to him. He looked younger and more energetic, often
spending his weekends teaching my youngest sister how to handle the delicate springs.
Looking at my parents now, as they enjoy their retirement in the comfort of their garden, I see a great
sense of satisfaction. The garden is filled with blooming flowers and the gentle sound of a grandfather
clock Dad fixed recently. The struggle of the early years hasn't been forgotten; rather, it has been a part
of our family history that we discuss over tea. Sitting on the patio, watching him carefully oil a gear while
Mum tends to her plants, I realise that the silence between thèm isn't empty—it is the peaceful quiet of a
family that is finally, perfectly happy.

How the Recycling Symbol Was Created
Today, the recycling symbol is recognised all over the world, yet most people do not know who
created it or how it first appeared. Gary Anderson designed the symbol in the early 1970s, when
environmental awareness in the United States was starting to increase rapidly. 27
As a university student, Anderson originally studied engineering at the University of Southern
California. 28
However, he soon realised that electronics was not his strength and decided to
switch to architecture instead. He felt that architecture allowed him to be both creative and practical at
the same time.
While studying, he entered a national competition to design a symbol related to recycling. The
competition was open to students across the country and attracted many creative ideas. He later
discovered that he had won through a letter sent to his home address. 29
He had taken part in
other contests before, so this felt like just another achievement. The prize included a modest amount of
money, although he can no longer remember the exact figure.
After graduating, Anderson decided to work in urban planning and moved to Los Angeles. He
focused on building his professional career rather than promoting his earlier success. In fact, he rarely
mentioned the recycling symbol during job interviews. As a result, many employers were unaware of his
contribution. For a period of time, the symbol seemed to fade from public attention. Then, during a
holiday trip to Amsterdam, he experienced an unforgettable moment. As soon as he stepped off the plane,
he noticed his symbol printed on a large recycling bin at the airport. 30
Years later, as his career developed, he began to reflect on the design itself. 31
To
improve it, he shifted certain elements slightly off-centre so that the symbol appeared more dynamic
and three-dimensional.
student.

The World of Sport
A - Sofia, 26 years old
Competitive sports are as much a mental challenge as a physical one. I work with athletes to develop
the winner's mindset. I teach techniques like visualization and stress management to help players
remain calm under intense pressure. By focusing on mental strength, athletes can overcome anxiety
and maintain peak concentration during crucial moments in a tournament or match.
B - Lee, 27 years old
Maintaining the integrity of professional sports is vital. I ensure that all competitors follow strict rules
regarding prohibited substances. I conduct random tests to catch those who try to gain an unfair
advantage. As an anti-doping officer, my work protects the spirit of fair play, ensuring that victories are
earned through hard work and natural talent rather than chemical assistance or illegal medical
enhancements.
C - Nabila, 23 years old
Modern coaching relies heavily on statistics to improve team performance. My colleagues and I use
advanced software to track every movement, pass, and goal during a game. By studying these numbers,
we can identify a player's weaknesses or predict an opponent's next move. This scientific approach
allows teams to create better strategies and make informed decisions that could lead to a championship
victory.
D - Nafis, 28 years old
Large sporting facilities often consume massive amounts of energy. I am now focusing on making
stadiums more environmentally friendly by installing solar panels and rainwater harvesting systems. I
work together with my friends to implement recycling programs for fans during major games. Our goal
is to reduce the carbon footprint of the sports industry, showing that entertainment events can be
sustainable and protect our planet.
E - Ramesh, 26 years old
Coaching teenagers requires more than just teaching technical skills; it involves organizing local
tournaments to build character. My team emphasizes teamwork, discipline, and respect for opponents.
We encourage young people to stay active while learning how to handle both success and failure
gracefully. Our influence helps shape the leaders of tomorrow through the universal language of
physical sport.
F - Shabina, 24 years old
Reporting on games requires a deep understanding of the sport and the ability to tell a compelling story.
Sports journalists like myself interview players and provide live commentary for fans worldwide. We
must remain objective while capturing the excitement of the stadium. Our work connects the public to
their sporting heroes, providing insights beyond the field
